items.title: Find the log line that matters faster with full-text search in Grafana Cloud Logs
items.summary: A support ticket comes in with one clue: a transaction ID. The answer is somewhere in your logs, but you don't know which service logged it, which pod handled it, or which day it happened. So you write the query you always write, {service="payments"} |= "txn-123456", widen the time range to the last two weeks, and wait. Then the query times out.Loki was originally built around a simple idea: index labels, not log content, and store compressed logs cheaply in object storage. That design keeps storage costs low and operations light, and it's why teams keep choosing Loki and Grafana Cloud Logs, the fully managed log aggregation system powered by Loki, as their log volumes grow. For most queries, this model works very well. But when you search for a highly unique value, like a request ID, job ID, user ID, or device ID, labels can only narrow the search so far. Loki still has to read a lot of raw log data to find a handful of matching lines. At terabyte and petabyte scale, that process can be slow and costly.To fix that, we built full-text search for Grafana Cloud Logs, a capability based on the Logline technology Grafana Labs acquired in April 2026. Full-text search, now generally available in Grafana Cloud Logs, adds a purpose-built secondary index to Loki, so you can find specific log lines across weeks of logs in seconds without a full scan. You go straight to the one transaction ID, user ID, or error that matters and cut time to resolution. “When I ran our first query on newly submitted logs after enabling Logline, the improvement was clear,” said Timo Kirzdörfer, OpenTelemetry & Grafana Cloud Admin, DATEV eG. “We went from processing nearly a terabyte of logs in three minutes to around 100 gigabytes in under three seconds. That represents an 80-90% reduction in the volume of logs searched for newly submitted logs, and we saw the results immediately.”In this post, we’ll explore how full-text search speeds up log investigations. You can also learn more in the ObservabilityCON 2026 talk below.Why labels alone only get you so farHistorically, Loki only indexed labels, then scanned every line in the selected streams. That is fast when the selector and the time range are already narrow. Searching a wide selector over a long window for one request ID means reading all of those lines. If you've run Loki at scale, you've probably reached for one of these techniques to avoid that scan:Put the whole or partial ID in a label. This is an obvious fix, but it creates high cardinality. Request IDs and user IDs make so many unique streams that ingestion and query performance suffer and eventually hit configured limits. Loki's cardinality guidance warns against this for good reason.Shrink the time range and guess. This works if you already know roughly when something happened. During an incident, or with a ticket that came in days later, you usually don't.Send some logs to a separate full-text index. That means running a second system, paying to index every field, and making engineers switch tools mid-investigation.Full-text search removes that tradeoff. The secondary index tells Loki which data can contain a literal string, so Loki reads only that data and skips the rest. That makes a big difference in how much data a query scans and how fast it returns.And it does this without the overhead of a traditional inverted index. The Logline technology behind it adds approximately 10% to compute costs and 10% to storage at Grafana Cloud scale with the current capabilities. Much of that cost is offset by the query compute Loki saves by reading less data.Loki also stays schemaless. You keep your labels and your ingestion pipelines, whether that's Alloy, the OpenTelemetry Collector, or another supported client, and you keep writing LogQL. For supported queries, searches that used to time out can now return in seconds or less.Find answers faster with full-text search Full-text search accelerates several LogQL patterns used for needle-in-a-haystack lookups:Exact string matches, using |=.Literal regex searches, using |~, including case-sensitive searches and case-insensitive searches with (?i).Label filter expressions over structured metadata and label attributes, such as | transaction_id="12345".Post-parser literal expressions over extracted attributes, such as | json | transaction_id="12345".Some advanced regex constructions are not supported; see the full-text search documentation for details.These patterns above support investigations ranging from following a transaction ID to tracking down an intermittent error.
